problemText: Alfred Wegener proposed that all of Earth's continents were once joined together in a single landmass. What did Wegener call this ancient supercontinent?
choices: Atlantis
Pangaea
Laurasia
Gondwana
hints: The lesson uses this specific name when introducing Wegener's 1912 proposal.
This term comes from the Greek words for 'all' and 'Earth.'

problemText: A scientist finds that the coastline of western Africa has a curved indentation, and the coastline of eastern South America has a corresponding curved bulge that fits into that indentation like puzzle pieces. Why is this shape match significant evidence for continental drift rather than just an interesting coincidence?
choices: Coastlines are made of the same type of rock on both continents, which proves they formed at the same time and must have been connected.
The two continents are close enough to each other geographically that they could still be moving toward one another through forces we can measure today.
Coastline shapes are random features that should not match between distant continents unless they were once joined together.
The matching coastline shapes occur along with similar mountain ranges and rock formations that run parallel to both coasts, suggesting the continents fit together like puzzle pieces.
hints: Think about whether coastline shapes should naturally match on continents thousands of kilometers apart.
The lesson explains why this particular kind of evidence (a shape match) would not happen by accident.

problemText: Lystrosaurus was a land animal that could not swim across an ocean. Fossils of Lystrosaurus are found in matching-age rock layers in South America, southern Africa, and India—three continents that are now separated by open ocean. What does the presence of Lystrosaurus on all three continents suggest about the past positions of these landmasses?
choices: The three continents have always been in their current positions, but Lystrosaurus lived only during a time when sea levels were much lower.
Lystrosaurus must have been a stronger swimmer than scientists originally thought, and it crossed the oceans on its own.
Ocean currents carried eggs or juveniles of Lystrosaurus across the ocean, where they grew into adult animals.
The three continents were once close enough together or connected for Lystrosaurus to walk between them without crossing ocean water.
hints: Remember that Lystrosaurus could not swim across open ocean—so how else could it reach all three continents?
The lesson shows that organisms without the ability to cross oceans on their own fossil locations tell us about how continents were arranged.

problemText: Scientists studying the floor of the Atlantic Ocean near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge discover that the pattern of magnetic stripes in the rock on the western side of the ridge is a mirror image of the stripe pattern on the eastern side. The rock closest to the ridge is younger, and rock farther away on both sides is progressively older. What do these two observations together tell us about the Atlantic Ocean floor?
choices: New ocean floor rock is forming at the ridge and spreading outward on both sides over time, so the ocean floor itself is moving.
The Atlantic Ocean floor is stationary and has always been in its current position beneath the water.
The magnetic field at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is stronger than it is anywhere else on Earth's ocean floors.
The oldest rocks on the Atlantic Ocean floor are located directly at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and younger rocks are found farther away.
hints: Consider why rock at the ridge would be younger than rock farther away, and what that pattern means for how the seafloor is created.
The mirror-image pattern and the age pattern work together to show a process—what is that process telling us?

problemText: Wegener's evidence from matching coastlines, fossils, and rock layers strongly suggested that continents had moved, yet most scientists rejected his idea. Decades later, the discovery of mirror-image magnetic stripe patterns on the seafloor finally convinced the scientific community to accept continental drift. Why did the magnetic stripe evidence succeed where Wegener's earlier evidence had failed to convince most scientists?
choices: The magnetic stripe patterns were found at greater depths in the ocean than fossil evidence, making them more resistant to erosion and therefore more reliable over geological time.

The stripe patterns proved that the ocean floor itself forms and moves, showing a physical mechanism by which continental movement could occur, rather than only showing that continents fit together or once carried the same organisms.
Scientists realized that Wegener's fossil and coastline evidence had actually been incorrect all along, but the magnetic stripes on the ocean floor revealed the true history of continental positions.
The stripe patterns revealed a specific driving force for continental motion, identifying convection currents in the mantle as the mechanism that Wegener could never adequately explain.
hints: The lesson states that Wegener's guesses about what moves continents were shown to be too weak—what new piece of information did the seafloor stripes provide?
Think about the difference between evidence that continents once fit together and evidence that shows how the ocean floor itself is created and moves.

problemText: A geologist finds that a sequence of five rock layers, formed in the same order and dated to the same age, appears in both a mountain region of South America and a mountain region of southern Africa. At the same time, she discovers fossils of Glossopteris (a seed fern with heavy seeds that cannot be blown far by wind) in layers at both locations. She also notes that these two mountain regions have matching coastline shapes when their present-day continental outlines are placed side by side. Should she conclude that South America and southern Africa were once joined? Explain why or why not, using all three types of evidence.
choices: Yes, she should conclude they were once joined, but only because of the fossil evidence of Glossopteris; rock layers can form separately in different locations, and matching coastlines are common features on many continents today.

No, she should not conclude they were once joined. While one of these observations might suggest a connection, individual types of evidence can result from coincidence or independent processes, so a single matching feature proves nothing definitive.

Yes, she should conclude they were once joined. Three independent types of evidence—matching rock-layer sequences, matching fossil distributions of an organism that could not disperse widely, and matching coastline shapes—all point to the same conclusion, making the case stronger than any single line of evidence alone.

No, she should not conclude they were once joined. The Glossopteris fossils and matching rocks prove the continents were connected at one time, but the matching coastlines contradict this and indicate the continents were never in contact.
hints: The lesson emphasizes that Wegener built his case using several separate kinds of evidence that all pointed the same direction—what does it mean when multiple independent lines of clue agree?
Consider whether each type of evidence (rocks, fossils, and coastlines) is truly independent, and whether multiple agreements make the conclusion stronger or weaker.

problemText: Earth's lithosphere is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. Which layer of Earth do these plates rest on and move across?
choices: The outer core, which is liquid metal that exists beneath the entire lithosphere and carries plates along as it circulates
The crust, which is a thick, rigid layer made of solid rock that is strong enough to support and anchor the tectonic plates from directly below
The asthenosphere, a layer of solid rock in the mantle that flows extremely slowly
A layer of liquid magma that sits between the crust and core, allowing plates to slide across its molten surface without friction
hints: Remember: the layer below the lithosphere is part of the mantle, not the core.
The material beneath the plates is solid rock, not liquid, even though it moves over time.

problemText: A scientist measures the location of a tectonic plate boundary using instruments on both sides of it. One year later, she measures again and finds the two sides have moved 3 centimeters farther apart. Which statement best explains why this happened?
choices: The lithosphere at that location fractured due to pressure buildup, and the cracks allowed the two sides to separate and move apart
The continental crust at the boundary was eroded by wind and water over the year, removing rock that had held the plates together
The asthenosphere suddenly became less viscous and behaved more like a liquid, reducing friction and allowing rapid plate movement
Mantle convection, a slow circulating pattern of rock motion deep in Earth, is carrying the plates apart
hints: Think about what process moves all of Earth's plates, as described in the lesson.
The plates are being carried along by motion in the layer beneath them, not broken apart by surface events.

problemText: The Pacific Plate is one of Earth's largest tectonic plates. A student claims the Pacific Plate must carry the entire continent of Asia on top of it, since it is so enormous. Is that claim correct, and why?
choices: No, the claim is wrong because the Pacific Plate is almost entirely ocean floor, with no full continent riding on it
No, the claim is wrong because Asia sits on multiple different plates rather than being carried by a single massive plate
Yes, the claim is correct because large plates always carry large landmasses to maintain Earth's gravitational balance
Yes, the claim is correct because size and composition are the only factors that determine what a plate can support
hints: Recall what the lesson said about what kinds of crust can be part of a single tectonic plate.
A plate's size is not determined by whether a continent sits on top of it.

problemText: Two neighboring tectonic plates are spreading apart at a rate of 5 centimeters per year. The lesson describes mantle convection as the slow, circulating pattern of motion that carries these plates along. Approximately how much farther apart will these two plates be after 2 million years, and what is driving that motion?
choices: About 1,000 kilometers farther apart, driven by liquid magma under the lithosphere
About 100 kilometers farther apart, driven by mantle convection powered by energy deep inside Earth
About 10 kilometers farther apart, driven by the rotation of Earth's core
About 100,000 kilometers farther apart, driven by the cooling and contracting of the crust
hints: Start by converting: 5 cm/year times 2 million years. Write out 2 million as a full number, then multiply and convert to kilometers.
The lesson explains what drives the plates' motion—it is not magma, Earth's rotation, or crustal cooling.

problemText: A student states: 'The boundary between the North American Plate and the Atlantic Ocean is at the East Coast of the United States, where the continent meets the ocean water.' Evaluate this statement using what you know about tectonic plates and lithosphere.
choices: The statement is correct because tectonic plate boundaries are always located at coastlines where the continent meets the ocean, and this is where geological activity occurs
The statement is correct because continental crust belongs to one plate and ocean crust belongs to a different plate, so plate boundaries must exist wherever they meet at the coastline
The statement is wrong because the North American Plate extends far out under the Atlantic Ocean floor, and its true boundary with a neighboring plate is much farther east than the coastline
The statement is wrong because the North American Plate is completely separate from the ocean floor beneath the Atlantic, and the true boundary lies somewhere inland, not at the coast
hints: A tectonic plate is made of lithosphere, which includes both continental and ocean-floor crust sitting on the same slab.
Recall that the North American Plate carries part of the Atlantic Ocean floor as one connected piece with the continent.

problemText: A geology class investigates two claims about Earth's plates and mantle. Claim 1: 'The asthenosphere is liquid magma that floats the lithosphere on top of it, the way a raft floats on water.' Claim 2: 'The asthenosphere is solid rock that flows extremely slowly, and mantle convection is a slow, circulating pattern of motion in that solid rock.' Using only what the lesson teaches, which claim is supported by evidence, what specific misunderstanding does the wrong claim show, and why does the distinction matter for understanding how plates move?
choices: Claim 1 is correct; Claim 2 is wrong because solid material cannot move at all, and plates can only be transported across Earth's surface if they float on liquid, the way boats float on water
Claim 1 is supported by evidence; Claim 2 misunderstands the nature of the asthenosphere because it ignores that liquid magma beneath the plates is what actually causes them to shift and move
Both claims describe the same process using different words, and the distinction between liquid and solid material does not affect how plates move or how mantle convection carries them

Claim 2 is correct; Claim 1 wrongly treats the asthenosphere as liquid when it is solid; this matters because plates resting on solid, flowing rock are dragged along by the convection pattern, not floated by a liquid layer
hints: The lesson specifically corrects the 'liquid magma ocean' picture and explains what the asthenosphere actually is.
Think about how a plate can be 'carried along' by mantle convection if the rock beneath it is solid but moving in a slow, circulating pattern.

problemText: At a plate boundary, two plates are moving away from each other and the distance between them is growing. What type of boundary is this?
choices: Sliding
Convergent
Transform
Divergent
hints: Think about what the word 'divergent' means — does it match plates moving apart or together?
Check whether the distance between the plates is growing, shrinking, or staying the same.

problemText: Scientists track two points on the ocean floor, one on each side of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Over time, the western point moves west and the eastern point moves east. The distance between the two points increases every year. Based on this motion alone, which type of boundary marks the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
choices: Divergent, because the two points are moving in opposite directions away from each other
Convergent, because the two points are moving toward each other and the distance between them is decreasing over time
Transform, because the two points are moving at the same speed in opposite directions along a fault line
Convergent, because the points are on opposite sides of a boundary and moving in opposite directions
hints: The key is not that the points move in opposite directions, but whether the gap between them is growing, shrinking, or staying the same.
Look at the trend over time: does the distance increase, decrease, or stay constant?

problemText: At the San Andreas Fault in California, the Pacific plate slides north while the North American plate slides south, both moving along the line of the fault. Measurements show the distance across the fault, from west to east, has remained about the same for the past hundred years. What type of boundary is the San Andreas Fault?
choices: Convergent, because the two plates are moving toward each other and closing the gap across the fault
Transform, because the plates slide past each other and the distance across the boundary stays the same
Divergent, because the plates are moving in opposite directions and pulling away from each other
Transform, because the two sides move in different directions while the east-west distance remains constant
hints: Remember that 'different directions' does not automatically mean the plates are closing in — check whether they are moving toward or past each other across the boundary.
Is the distance across the fault growing, shrinking, or staying about the same? That is what decides the type.

problemText: A boundary runs along the edge of a continent. On one side is a plate carrying open ocean floor; on the other side is a plate carrying the continent. Surveys show these two plates have been moving toward each other for millions of years, and the distance between them is shrinking. Another scientist observes that one side is not a continent but ocean floor, so she suggests this cannot be a convergent boundary. Explain why she is wrong using only the motion data.
choices: It is convergent only because a plate carrying ocean floor is involved, not because of the direction of motion
It cannot be convergent because convergent boundaries only occur where two continental plates collide, and ocean floor plates always move away from continents rather than toward them
A convergent boundary is defined by the two plates moving toward each other and the gap between them shrinking, regardless of whether either plate carries a continent or ocean floor.

The scientist is correct — a boundary is only convergent if both sides carry continental material, so this boundary must be classified as a different type based on the composition of the plates involved
hints: The lesson teaches that a plate boundary is named by direction of motion alone, not by what each plate carries.
What is the one question that decides a boundary's type? Does the answer depend on what material each plate carries?

problemText: Two plate boundaries are observed. Boundary X shows one plate moving north and the other plate moving south, with the two plates sliding along the boundary line. Boundary Y shows one plate moving east and the other plate moving west, with the distance between the two plates decreasing every year. Which statement correctly describes these boundaries?
choices: Boundary X is transform and Boundary Y is divergent because the motion at each boundary is different from the other.
Boundary X is convergent and Boundary Y is transform because they show opposite direction pairs.
Boundary X is convergent because the plates move in opposite directions, and Boundary Y is divergent because the plates move in opposite directions.
Boundary X is transform because the plates slide past each other, and Boundary Y is convergent because the plates are closing the gap between them.
hints: For Boundary X: are the plates moving toward each other, away from each other, or sliding past one another? Check the distance across the boundary.
For Boundary Y: is the gap between the plates growing, shrinking, or staying the same? That measurement decides the type.

problemText: A student observes three plate boundaries and notes the following: Boundary P — the two sides move in different directions; Boundary Q — the distance between the two plates grows each year; Boundary R — the two sides move in the same direction along the boundary line. The student concludes, 'Any time two plate sides move in different directions, it must be a convergent boundary where the two sides are crashing together.' Use evidence from the lesson to show that this conclusion is wrong and explain which boundary type actually matches plates moving in different directions without crashing.
choices: The conclusion is wrong because different directions alone does not tell you whether the plates are converging; Boundary P could be transform if the plates slide past each other while the distance across the boundary stays the same, which is moving in different directions without crashing.

The conclusion is wrong because Boundary R, where two sides move in the same direction, shows plates sliding side-by-side, which is a transform boundary where the gap between plates remains constant even though motion occurs

The conclusion is wrong because plates that move in different directions always diverge rather than converge, making Boundary Q the only type where the shrinking distance indicates plates are actually crashing together

The conclusion is wrong because Boundary P must be divergent since the plates move in opposite directions, and only at divergent boundaries do plates move away from each other without any collision or compression between them
hints: The lesson emphasizes a trap: different directions does not equal convergent. What measurement actually decides whether plates are crashing or sliding?
Think about transform boundaries like the San Andreas Fault: do the two sides move in different directions? Is the distance across the boundary growing, shrinking, or staying the same?

problemText: A fold mountain range forms when two plates carrying continental crust collide head-on. Why does neither plate sink beneath the other in this collision?
choices: Continental crust is too close in density on both sides, so neither plate is dense enough to subduct.
Continental crust is much lighter than oceanic crust, so both plates float upward instead of sinking.
The two plates are moving too slowly to allow subduction to occur.
Fold mountains always form above a transform boundary where plates slide past each other.
hints: Recall what determines whether a plate will sink at a convergent boundary.
Think about how the density of the two plates compares to each other in this scenario.

problemText: A deep underwater trench has just been discovered alongside a chain of volcanic islands in the middle of an ocean. Both plates meeting at this boundary are made of ocean floor. Which of the following best explains why these two landforms appear together at the same location?
choices: The trench is a gap where new ocean floor is being added from magma rising between the plates, and the islands are old volcanic mountains that formed before the plates started moving in this direction.
The trench marks where the denser oceanic plate bends down and sinks, while melted rock from that sinking plate rises through the plate above it and erupts as volcanoes on the islands.
The islands form where magma rises continuously as one plate sinks, and the volcanoes build up above sea level, while the trench deepens as the plate continues to bend downward into the mantle.
The trench and islands are both results of plates sliding sideways past each other, with the friction from the sliding motion generating enough heat to melt rock and create the volcanic islands.
hints: Identify whether this boundary is pushing plates together or pulling them apart.
Remember what happens to the melted rock when one oceanic plate sinks beneath another.

problemText: Along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, two oceanic plates are moving away from each other. Magma rises up into the gap between them and hardens into new ocean-floor rock. Over millions of years, this process is slowly widening the Atlantic Ocean. What is this underwater mountain chain called, and what type of plate boundary created it?
choices: A rift valley formed by a divergent boundary where two continental plates stretch apart.
A volcanic island arc formed by a convergent boundary where two oceanic plates collide.
A mid-ocean ridge formed by a divergent boundary where two oceanic plates pull apart.
An ocean trench formed by a convergent boundary where oceanic crust sinks beneath continental crust.
hints: Notice that this process involves plates moving apart and magma filling a gap, not plates colliding.
Consider whether this boundary involves oceanic plates, continental plates, or a mix of the two.

problemText: A geologist observes a region where two plates carrying continental crust are pushing directly toward each other along a convergent boundary. She notes that neither plate is sinking beneath the other, and the crust in the region is being thickened and pushed upward into high mountains that are still being raised today, much like the Himalayas. Based on what you know about plate density and subduction, explain why this outcome—thickened, uplifted crust instead of subduction—must occur at this type of boundary.
choices: Transform boundaries along continental crust always produce uplifted mountains because the sideways sliding motion prevents subduction and forces rock to crumple and pile up instead.
Continental crust is less dense than oceanic crust everywhere on Earth, so both colliding plates float and rise equally when pushed, causing the rock between them to buckle upward into mountains.
The plates are moving too slowly to subduct, so over time the friction between them causes the rock to heat up and expand, which pushes the crust upward and thickens it into mountain ranges.
Continental crust is too similar in density on both sides to allow one plate to sink, so the rock crumples and stacks upward instead, thickening the crust and building mountains.
hints: Think about what decides whether a plate will subduct at a convergent boundary—what property of the plates matters most.
Recall that subduction only happens when one plate is clearly denser than the other and can be pulled downward.

problemText: Two different convergent boundaries are being compared. At Boundary X, two oceanic plates collide, with one denser than the other. At Boundary Y, an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate, with the oceanic plate being the denser one. Which boundary will produce an ocean trench, and which will produce fold mountains? Explain your reasoning based on which plates can subduct and what happens to the crust above the subducting plate.
choices: Boundary X produces a trench and volcanic island arc because both plates are oceanic and the denser one sinks; Boundary Y produces fold mountains because continental crust is too thick to subduct fully and instead crumples upward.

Boundary Y produces a trench because oceanic crust is always denser than continental crust, so it can subduct beneath it; Boundary X produces fold mountains because two similar oceanic plates lack a clear density difference to drive subduction.
Both boundaries produce trenches because whenever oceanic crust is present at a convergent boundary, it is dense enough to sink, and subduction must occur at that location.

Boundary X produces fold mountains because oceanic plates are too similar in density to subduct; Boundary Y produces a trench because the oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate and creates a deep ocean basin.
hints: Recall what happens when both plates at a convergent boundary are oceanic versus when one is oceanic and one is continental.
Think about whether fold mountains form when one plate clearly can subduct or when no plate can sink.

problemText: A continental rift valley is currently being pulled apart by two diverging plates. A geologist studying the valley notes that the floor of the valley sits lower than the surrounding land, and the sides show raised edges with cracks running along them. She also notes that if this rift continues to widen for millions of years, ocean water might eventually move into the valley floor. Based on your understanding of how rift valleys form and how they change over time, explain why ocean water would eventually be able to enter the valley, and identify a real-world example where this has already happened.
choices: As the valley widens, the exposed rock at the bottom becomes softer and weathered, which allows erosion to deepen the valley floor faster than the plates can continue to pull apart.
As the continental plates pull apart and the valley floor stretches and drops lower, it can eventually sink below sea level; the Red Sea is a rift valley that widened until ocean water moved in.
The continental crust beneath the valley becomes thinner and is eventually replaced by oceanic crust, which is denser and heavier, causing it to sink below sea level and allow ocean water to enter.

The valley floor will gradually fill with sediment from erosion on the surrounding highlands, and when enough sediment builds up, it will reach high enough to allow ocean water to flow into the valley from the sides.
hints: Consider what happens to the elevation of the valley floor as the two continental plates continue to diverge over a very long time.
Recall the definition of a rift valley and what the lesson says about what can happen if it keeps widening.
